common_name: Sam Barlow Dianthus (Heirloom White Pink with Near-Black Center)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Sam Barlow is a British heirloom pink named for the allotment gardener who grew and distributed it, prized for its dramatic near-black eye.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Sam Barlow carries fully double, pure white flowers centered on a strikingly dark maroon-black eye that gives the whole bloom a bold, high-contrast look unusual among old-fashioned pinks, backed by a strong, sweet clove scent. The low, tidy mound of blue-gray foliage stays attractive through the season and makes a dependable edging plant once established in sharp drainage. Shear lightly after the main spring flush to tidy the foliage mat and encourage further bloom.

common_name: Queen of Sheba Dianthus (White Laced Purple-Maroon Heritage Pink)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Queen of Sheba is an old laced pink grown for its intricate contrasting lacing pattern.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Queen of Sheba is a heritage laced pink, its white semi-double petals overlaid near the base with a fine, deep purple-maroon pattern that radiates outward in the classic 'laced' style once bred extensively by English florists' societies. Flowers carry a spicy clove fragrance and appear in a concentrated spring flush above a compact, blue-green foliage mound. Shear lightly once the main bloom fades to keep the mat dense and encourage tidy regrowth.

common_name: Valda Wyatt Dianthus (AGM Double Lilac-Pink Fragrant Pink)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Valda Wyatt holds a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit and is valued for exceptionally fragrant, long-lasting double flowers.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Valda Wyatt bears large, fully double, soft lilac-pink flowers with a neat, rounded form and an intensely sweet clove fragrance that carries well across a border, blooming over an unusually long season for a garden pink when deadheaded regularly. The dense, silvery blue-green foliage mound stays attractive between bloom flushes and holds up well through summer heat. Shear lightly after the first main flush to keep growth compact and to encourage repeat flowering into late summer.

common_name: Whatfield Magenta Dianthus (Compact Alpine Pink with Vivid Magenta Flowers)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, gritty, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Whatfield Magenta is a compact alpine pink from the Whatfield series bred for rock gardens and trough plantings.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun, such as a scree bed, trough, or rock garden crevice. Whatfield Magenta forms a tight, low cushion of fine, needle-like blue-green foliage studded in late spring with small, single, vividly magenta-pink flowers held just above the mat. Its dwarf, dense habit makes it far more compact than typical border pinks, suiting intensively drained alpine plantings where larger cultivars would sprawl. Avoid winter wet and rich soil, both of which encourage rot and loose, less tidy growth.

common_name: Inshriach Dazzler Dianthus (Alpine Pink with Unusual Coral-Orange Flowers)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, gritty, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; Inshriach Dazzler takes its name from the Scottish alpine nursery where it was raised and is notable for flower color unusual in the genus.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, lean soil in full sun, ideally in a scree bed or raised rock garden where winter moisture drains away quickly. Inshriach Dazzler forms a low, tight mat of narrow blue-green foliage topped in late spring with single flowers in an unusual coral to salmon-orange shade, a notably warmer tone than the pinks, reds, and whites typical of most alpine dianthus. Its compact, slow-spreading habit suits troughs and crevice plantings where its distinctive color can be appreciated up close. Protect from winter wet and avoid overly rich soil, which weakens the tight alpine habit.

common_name: Telstar Crimson Dianthus (Compact Interspecific Pink with Vivid Crimson Blooms)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or plant nursery starts a few weeks before to shortly after the last frost into full sun; Telstar is an interspecific hybrid between Sweet William and China Pink bred for hardiness and heavy branching.

directions: Plant nursery-grown starts or direct seedlings into well-drained soil in full sun. Telstar Crimson is part of the AAS-winning Telstar series, an interspecific dianthus hybrid combining the hardiness and floriferousness of Sweet William with the compact habit and season-long bloom of China Pink, producing dense, vivid crimson-red single flowers with a light clove scent across a tidy, well-branched mound. The series blooms heavily from spring through fall without deadheading and tolerates summer heat better than older bedding dianthus strains. Keep soil well-drained, since dianthus is prone to crown rot in wet conditions.

common_name: Telstar White Dianthus (Compact Interspecific Pink with Pure White Blooms)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before the last frost, or plant nursery starts a few weeks before to shortly after the last frost into full sun; Telstar is an interspecific hybrid between Sweet William and China Pink bred for hardiness and heavy branching.

directions: Plant nursery-grown starts or direct seedlings into well-drained soil in full sun. Telstar White is part of the AAS-winning Telstar series, an interspecific dianthus hybrid combining the hardiness and floriferousness of Sweet William with the compact habit and season-long bloom of China Pink, producing clean, pure white single flowers with a light clove scent that brighten mixed beds and containers. The series blooms heavily from spring through fall without deadheading and tolerates summer heat better than older bedding dianthus strains. Keep soil well-drained, since dianthus is prone to crown rot in wet conditions.

common_name: Diana Scarlet Dianthus (Heat-Tolerant Bedding China Pink with Bright Scarlet Flowers)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or set out nursery transplants a few weeks before to shortly after the last frost into full sun; Diana Scarlet belongs to the Diana series, a compact bedding strain bred for large flowers and summer heat tolerance.

directions: Plant nursery-grown starts or direct seedlings into well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Diana Scarlet forms a dense, uniform mound of narrow gray-green foliage covered in unusually large, single, bright scarlet-red flowers for a China Pink strain, blooming from late spring through summer and holding up better in hot weather than many older bedding dianthus. Deadheading spent flowers keeps the compact plants tidy and encourages continued bloom into fall. Avoid heavy, wet soils, which quickly lead to crown rot in this shallow-rooted annual.

common_name: Pink Mrs Sinkins Dianthus (Fragrant Double Pink Sport of Mrs. Sinkins)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in fall in very well-drained, slightly alkaline to neutral soil in full sun; Pink Mrs Sinkins is a pink-flowered sport of the Victorian heirloom Mrs. Sinkins, sharing its parent's dense double form and heavy clove scent.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, lean, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Pink Mrs Sinkins carries the same fully double, heavily fringed flower form and intense sweet clove fragrance as the classic white Mrs. Sinkins, but opens in a soft rose-pink rather than white, giving collectors a color option on an otherwise identical heirloom habit. It forms a low mat of gray-green foliage that remains tidy between bloom cycles and performs best where drainage is sharp and winters are not overly wet. Shear lightly after the main spring bloom to maintain a dense mound and encourage a possible second flush.

common_name: Spotty Dianthus (Compact Bedding China Pink with Contrasting Center Spot)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, or direct-sow after the last frost into full sun; Spotty is a longtime All-America Selections winning bedding strain grown for its uniquely marked flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Spotty produces compact, free-flowering plants whose single blooms each carry a distinct, contrasting spot or eye at the center in shades of pink, red, and white, giving the mixed strain a dotted, patterned look across a planting rather than the uniform solid colors of most bedding dianthus. Plants stay low and well-branched, making them useful for edging and containers, and bloom over a long stretch from late spring into summer. Deadhead regularly to prolong flowering and avoid wet, poorly drained soil, which encourages crown rot.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost or direct-sow in spring into well-drained soil in full sun; this Balkan native is the only dianthus species with yellow flowers.

directions: Plant in well-drained, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun. Dianthus knappii is the one species in the genus with yellow flowers, bearing small, pale yellow blooms in dense, branched clusters atop upright stems above narrow green foliage, a distinctly different look from the typical mat-forming, clove-scented pinks. It is shorter-lived than many perennial dianthus and benefits from occasional division or replacement from seed every few years to maintain vigor. Give it sharp drainage and avoid rich, wet soils, which shorten its already modest lifespan.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost or direct-sow in spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Carthusian pink is a European meadow species popular in naturalistic and gravel plantings.

directions: Plant in lean, well-drained soil in full sun; this species thrives in poor, gravelly ground and declines in rich or overly moist sites. Carthusian pink sends up slender, wiry stems well above a low tuft of grassy foliage, each topped with a tight cluster of small, vivid magenta-pink flowers that bloom over a long stretch of early to midsummer. Its upright, airy habit reads differently in the border than mat-forming dianthus species, weaving naturally among grasses and other meadow perennials. Established plants self-sow readily in favorable lean soils, helping maintain a colony over time.

planting.note: Direct-sow in late summer or fall for a basal rosette that overwinters and flowers the following summer, or sow in early spring for bloom the second year; Deptford pink is a European species long naturalized in meadows and roadsides across eastern North America.

directions: Sow directly in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where it is unfussy about soil fertility. Deptford pink is a slender biennial or short-lived perennial, forming a low rosette in its first season before sending up wiry, branched stems the next year topped with small, deep pink flowers flecked with tiny white spots, clustered in groups of a few blooms at a time. It is at home in informal meadow plantings and along sunny field edges rather than formal borders, and it self-sows freely once established, maintaining itself from year to year without replanting. Avoid fertile, heavily amended soil, which produces floppy, less floriferous growth.

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost or direct-sow in spring into sandy, sharply drained soil in full sun; sand pink is a Baltic and Scandinavian native adapted to coastal and inland sand habitats.

directions: Plant in sandy, sharply drained, lean soil in full sun, mimicking the native dune and sand-barren habitats of this species. Sand pink forms a low, dense cushion of fine, grassy foliage covered in midsummer with fragrant white flowers whose petals are cut into narrow, deeply fringed segments, giving each bloom a delicate, almost lacy appearance. It is notably more tolerant of pure sandy soils and summer drought than many other dianthus species, making it a good fit for coastal or xeric gardens. Avoid heavy or consistently moist soils, which are poorly tolerated by this sand-adapted species.
